A sealed biosphere of up to millions of particles, and all of them live, eat, breed, and die in your browser, simulated on the GPU with WebGPU. Some cells drink the moving light of the tide. Others graze on the photosynthesizers, and others hunt the grazers. Scavengers break down the dead and return them to the water as silt, and from that silt the next generation builds its children. Children mutate into new species. Species that bond grow into bodies: filaments, branched fronds, spirals, packed tissues. Some of these bodies grow beating tails and swim. Every 10 to 18 minutes the climate turns, and the world has to begin again in its own way. It makes its own music, too: each cell sings its species' song, over a chorus of the births, kills, and deaths in view. Leave the simulation running and it keeps changing for hours.

Tidemote is a sealed biosphere of up to millions of particles, and all of them live, eat, breed, and die in your browser, simulated on the GPU with WebGPU. Some cells drink the moving light of the tide. Others graze on the producers, and others hunt the grazers. Scavengers break down the dead and return them to the water as silt, and from that silt the next generation builds its children. Children mutate into new species. Species that bond grow into bodies: filaments, branched fronds, spirals, packed tissues. Some of these bodies grow beating tails and swim. Every 10 to 18 minutes the climate turns, and the world has to begin again in its own way. It makes its own music, too: each cell sings its species' song, over a chorus of the births, kills, and deaths in view. Leave the simulation running and it keeps changing for hours.

Producers are photosynthetic cells, anchored colonies and free-floating drifters alike. Consumers are grazers that crop them, scavengers of husks and dung, and predators. Every world founds each of these niches at least twice. Several pressures shape which forms thrive:
Anchored producers thrive where currents run strong; drifting ones where they are calm. Bonded bodies live cheaply and resist attack but disperse poorly.

Holds leftover energy for scavengers and crumbles back into silt after about half a minute: cold water keeps carcasses for the scavengers, warm water rots them fast, and a rotting pile warms its water a little.

Every 10–18 minutes the climate turns: the baseline light and the water’s temperature change, one tide wave is replaced, and the currents shift. In about one era in six the water stands low and the highest ground shows as islands of dry land; the next full-water era covers them again. An era that warms the water by 5° or more is named Warm or Rising, one that cools it Bitter or Pale; otherwise the names are random labels.

The water’s background temperature, set by the climate: it walks from era to era between 4° and 28°, swings ±2.5° with the season, and now and then a heat wave or cold snap passes. Life warms its own water above this: every cell’s spent energy becomes heat, so crowds sit in warm patches.

A pyrite framboid: a sphere of tiny iron sulfide crystals, a few microns across like the cells. Framboids grow where a pile of husks rots in cool water (the rot releases the sulfide), and a few lie in the mud from the start. As one oxidizes it warms its water, burning faster the warmer that water is, so a crowded, hot cluster burns itself out. Once spent, it crumbles to silt. Sparks of life favor their warmth, and heat-loving species gather round them. Framboids are solid like stone.

Eating other living cells. A cell can only eat species whose surface signature looks unlike its own. Caught animal prey are killed outright and leaves a husk; this takes time, so a hunter manages at most one kill every few seconds. Plant cells are cropped a 0.25-energy bite at a time. Bonded bodies are armored and shrug off some attacks, and an animal hiding among dense producers often escapes.

Nothing can eat a cyst. Cysts are the seed bank that carries a lineage through hard times.

Sand, and the skeletons of calcifying cells. Stone never drifts and the living cannot pass through it. Attacks made from among stone sometimes miss, so prey shelters in reefs, and calcifying cells settle on their own reef while everything else must go around it. Bedrock lasts nearly an hour. A loose grain of reef stone crumbles within minutes, a grain packed into a reef lasts far longer, and a neighborhood that is mostly reef wears fast, so reefs grow as separate patches and persist only while they are being built.

How much of a skeleton a cell lays down. Calcifying costs upkeep. When a settled calcifying cell dies of hunger or old age it may leave stone instead of a husk, far more often beside stone already there, so reefs grow outward from rock. Drifting cells seldom leave stone. Calcifiers can settle on stone; to everything else it is solid.

How strongly cells of one species bond. Above 15%, each cell keeps up to two same-species partners with springs. Empty slots find the nearest neighbors within bond range; children start bonded to their parent if they are the same species. Bonds last until a partner dies, changes kind, or stretches too far away. Bonds are the links you see and they hold bodies together. Bonded cells share the cost of living (up to 15% less upkeep), shade each other less and are armored against attack. They still pay crowding beyond their bond partners, disperse poorly and their inner cells struggle to reach silt to divide. Species without adhesion are single-celled.

How a bonded species builds its body, inherited and mutated like every other gene. Some grow as trees: each new cell buds from a tip at the angle the plan sets, branching every few cells (alternate, one-sided, opposite, or forking), a set number of orders deep, curling or zigzagging as they go, the way filamentous algae, branched cyanobacteria and colonial ciliates grow. The tips are fed by the cells behind them. Others pack into a body as their cells meet.

How much simulated time each step moves the world forward. Normally a step is 1/60 s, the most exact. When you ask for a speed the GPU can’t reach in steps that small, it takes bigger ones instead, up to 6/60 s; so does a device that can’t draw 60 frames a second, one step a frame (2/60 s at 30 fps). Bigger steps are a little coarser , but births, deaths and the variety of species stay the same over long runs.

What this cell is doing, read from a replay of its latest decision. A cell has no brain: every frame it adds up the pulls and pushes of everything within reach (its receptors against their surface signatures, appetite for the foods its diet favors, schooling, bonds, stone), moves, then eats, divides, or neither. The mode names which pull wins; hover it for the reasoning. The compass draws each pull as an arrow, its length the pull’s strength, with the cell’s heading dashed and its target as a diamond on the rim. The lamps light for conditions that shape what it does. Fleeing is an evolved aversion: no cell knows what a predator is, but lineages whose receptors happened to push them away from their hunters survived.

One map over the view at a time. Light colors every point by the light a photosynthesizing cell would get there; Heat is a thermal camera, deep blue to teal to amber to white over a span from 2° below the background water to 10° above it, with a contour line every 2°; Tide shows the light the Tide brings and where its bands are heading. Its key (G, E, H) or gauge opens it, and again closes it.
Warm water bends light like the air over a hot road. Off, the view holds still over warm water (boiling water still roils). Auto draws it, and Adaptation may turn it off while frames run late.

The temperature a species works best at (0–45°). It drifts by mutation, so lineages can follow the climate or find a warm or cold refuge. A spark of life creates a species suited to the water it sparked in.

Far below its optimum temperature (more than 1.25 tolerances) a cell goes torpid: it doesn't feed, swim, or divide. Torpid cells pay a quarter of their upkeep, dim in color, stop pulsing, and fall silent until the water warms again.

A dormant cell. An animal cell running out of energy with nothing to eat in reach may go dormant. It stops swimming and pulsing, turns gray, leaks only a little energy, and wakes at random, after about 45 seconds on average. Nothing can eat a cyst. Cysts are the seed bank that carries a lineage through hard times.

Sand, and the skeletons of calcifying cells. Stone never drifts and the living cannot pass through it. Attacks made from among stone sometimes miss, so prey shelters in reefs, and calcifying cells settle on their own reef while everything else must go around it. Sand in the pool at the start of a world lasts nearly an hour. A loose grain of reef stone crumbles within minutes and a tightly packed one lasts far longer, but a reef that spreads to fill most of the area around it wears away fast. So reefs stay as separate patches.

The simulation may reduce render quality if it is unable to maintain full quality at a smooth frame rate. This describes the reason: frames running late, the GPU busy for nearly the whole frame, the device under pressure (hot or busy, where the browser reports it), or the browser’s own pace (it hands out frames more slowly than the screen refreshes while the page has little to do: only the frame rate is lowered then). With Target fps on Auto it lowers the frame rate to 30 first, then eases what Adaptation may (work done less often, effects, the render scale), and below 30 only once nothing else is left. Adaptation will gradually restore quality if conditions improve, returning to 60 fps last.

Frames per second that the system is aiming for, as a whole number of the screen’s refreshes so frames stay evenly spaced. 30 FPS halves the GPU’s work and saves battery; Display follows the screen’s refresh rate (120 on many phones and Macs). Auto aims for 60 and, when the device can’t keep up, drops to 30 before easing anything else, and lower (20 or 15) only once nothing else is left (shown beside Auto); it returns to 60 last, once everything else is back. A rate chosen is held even then.

Every species has its own song, read from its genome. Its surface signature picks the notes, how it lives sets the rhythm, tempo and range (hunters leap in quick clipped figures, drifting photosynths sway through long ones), and its color picks the instrument. A mutant sings a variation: a few notes moved, or the tune turned upside down, reversed or answered. Its cells sing it as the, in step if the species schools; a bonded colony adds a second voice.

The <season>season</season> is a 5-minute cycle that swings tide strength between 10% and 100%. This is the Tide percentage shown in the gauge and graphs. The bands keep their shape; only their strengt changes. At high tide they are bright and the water is a little warmer. At low tide they fade until they are barely brighter than the rest of the world. This drives the regular booms and busts. Every 10–18 minutes an <era>era</era> begins: the baseline light changes, one tide wave is replaced so the bright zones form and move differently, and two current patterns are swapped. The water’s temperature walks from era to era, so each world has its own thermal history. Each era is named for what marks it as it begins: water warming or cooling, light rising or failing, the water falling to bare the floor or rising over it again, the pool’s last storm, drought, frost or duckweed, or the life that holds the pool (a bloom, a dwindling, hunters or grazers gaining, a genus reigning, a burst of new species). A kind of era that returns is counted (The Second Drowning), quiet stretches take stage names of the world’s own, and the event log says what actually changed.

The water has a temperature, and most of its warmth comes from life. Every unit of energy a cell spends on <upkeep>upkeep</upkeep> becomes heat in its water, so crowds, bodies, and reefs sit in warm patches of their own making. Heat also comes from sunlight (a little), from rotting carcass piles, and from <framboid>framboids</framboid>: grains of pyrite that crystallize in those piles and warm their water as they burn out over a few minutes, so a die-off leaves a warm oasis behind it for a while. Heat spreads a few cells, rides the currents (warm water trails downstream of a bloom) and relaxes toward the climate's <water>background</water> within about half a minute. Stone holds heat: reefs and bedrock warm and cool slowly.

Lab → Lineage: the lineages that held the most life, as a plot of their cells over time (each nested inside the lineage it branched from, so a die-off shows as the whole stack falling) over a tree of the same lineages. A lineage follows a population through species after species, and each row says how many species its lineage holds. Click a lineage’s row or its band in the plot to explore it, or drag across the plot to zoom into a stretch of time: finer lineages appear as you narrow in, down to single species. The reticle on the row you point at shows its species in the water, as does each name in an explored lineage’s line of descent. The path above the plot runs from all lineages down through the explored lineage’s ancestors, each a click to go up to; a narrowed span shows beside it, with × to widen it again; Esc or Backspace goes back the way you came.

Lab → Lineage: the family trees of the most successful species. A lineage is a line of descent, followed through every species it evolves into. The top shows each lineage’s cells over time, with every branch drawn inside the lineage it came from, so a die-off shows as the whole stack falling. The tree below lists the same lineages, each with how many species it holds. Click a row or a band to explore that lineage, or drag across the plot to zoom into a stretch of time. Smaller branches appear as you zoom in, down to single species. Point at a row and click its reticle to see where that species is in the water; the names in a lineage’s line of descent do the same. The path above the plot shows where you are: click any step to go back up. A zoomed time range shows beside it, and × resets it. Esc or Backspace goes back one step.

How much simulated time each step moves the world forward. Normally a step is 1/60 s, the most exact. At higher simulation speeds when the GPU can’t keep up, it takes bigger strides per step instead, up to 6/60 s. A device that runs the world at 30 fps needs to double the stride to keep the same speed (2/60 s). Bigger steps are a little coarser and interpolate cell actions, but births, deaths, and the variety of species stay roughly the same over long runs.

Energy is the only thing that enters and leaves. It enters in two forms. The first is <light>light</light>: the pool receives a different amount of background light every era, and is brightest in the bands of the <tide>Tide</tide>.
